GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

All five options are AI-generated - do not consider the possibility that a human wrote it. Read the text carefully and identify which model most likely produced it, based on writing style, structure, and phrasing.

{"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- TEXT ---
Swapping the car for your own two feet or two wheels on short trips is one of those small lifestyle shifts that quietly pays dividends across almost every part of daily life. The errands we tend to drive for, a quick run to the grocery store, a coffee a few blocks away, dropping something in the mail, are often the ones where a car offers the least real advantage. Once you start leaving the keys behind for these kinds of trips, the benefits accumulate in ways that are easy to feel but hard to notice until you look back.

The most immediate reward is financial. Every short drive burns fuel inefficiently, since engines are least economical when they are cold and stopping frequently, and the costs of insurance, maintenance, and tire wear quietly tick upward with every mile. Add in the occasional parking meter, garage fee, or parking ticket, and the true price of a two-mile hop to pick up dinner is a lot steeper than the gas gauge suggests. Walking costs nothing at all, and biking costs only the modest upkeep of a chain and a set of tires. Over a year, replacing even a handful of weekly short drives with human-powered trips can add up to real money that stays in your pocket instead of disappearing into the pump or a parking app.

The second benefit is that movement gets folded into your day without any extra effort. One of the biggest obstacles to regular exercise is scheduling it, carving out a block of time, changing clothes, driving to a gym, and then driving home again. When walking or biking is simply how you get where you were already going, the workout happens on its own. A fifteen-minute walk to the pharmacy and back is a half hour of light cardio you did not have to plan, and a short bike ride to meet a friend doubles as the kind of steady activity that keeps joints loose, moods lifted, and sleep deeper. The exercise feels less like a chore and more like a natural rhythm of living, which is exactly the kind of movement people tend to stick with over the long run.

Finally, moving slowly through your own neighborhood changes your relationship to it. From behind a windshield, a street is mostly an obstacle course of signals and other cars, and the shops, gardens, and small details along the way blur into scenery. On foot or on a bike, you actually see the new bakery that opened on the corner, the neighbor repainting their porch, the shortcut through the park you never knew existed. You run into people you know, exchange a few words with a shopkeeper, notice the seasons shifting in the trees overhead. These small encounters and observations build a sense of belonging to a place, and over time they turn the area around your home from a backdrop into a community you feel genuinely connected to. Taken together, the saved money, the effortless exercise, and the richer sense of place make short walks and rides feel less like a sacrifice and more like one of the easiest upgrades available to everyday life.
--- END ---
Output the JSON object described above, and nothing else.
